input:
Feedback control is a fundamental idea in process control, and the temperature loop on a process vessel is a classic example. In essence, the loop holds the vessel temperature close to its set point by adjusting the heat supply in response to the temperature actually measured, and it is helpful to follow the signal around the loop in order, from the sensor, through the controller, to the final element, before turning to the sign of the feedback.

The sensor measures the vessel contents temperature and converts it into a signal the controller can use. The position of the sensor determines what the loop actually controls: a sensor in the contents reports the contents temperature, whereas a sensor in a pocket reports the pocket temperature, which follows the contents with a lag.

The controller compares the measured temperature with the set point, and the difference is known as the deviation. From the deviation, the controller calculates a correction. A positive deviation and a negative deviation call for corrections in opposite directions, and the size of the correction follows the size of the deviation under the control law in use.

The final element receives the controller output and changes the heat supply to the vessel. In many cases the final element is a valve, together with its actuator, on the heating-medium line, while in other cases the heat is supplied by an electric heater and the final element varies the heater power. The loop acts only through the final element, so at its limit the loop has no authority over the temperature.

The feedback in the loop is negative, which means that the action of the controller opposes the deviation: when the temperature rises above the set point the heat supply is reduced, and when it falls below, the heat supply is increased. This opposing action returns the temperature towards the set point after a disturbance. Positive feedback, by contrast, would drive the temperature further from the set point, and it is not used for holding a temperature.
target:
Feedback control holds the temperature of a process vessel at its set point by acting on the heat supply in response to the measured temperature. The loop is followed in signal order: sensor, controller, final element, and the sign of the feedback.

The sensor measures the vessel temperature and converts the measurement into a signal the controller can use. Sensor position fixes what the loop controls. A sensor in the vessel contents reports the contents temperature; a sensor in a pocket reports the pocket temperature, which follows the contents temperature with a lag.

The controller compares the measured temperature with the set point. The difference between the two values is the deviation, and the controller calculates a correction from the deviation. A positive deviation and a negative deviation call for corrections in opposite directions, and the size of the correction follows the size of the deviation under the control law in use.

The final element receives the controller output and changes the heat supply to the vessel. Where the heating medium enters through a valve, the final element is that valve and its actuator; where an electric heater supplies the heat, the final element varies the heater power. The loop acts only through the final element, and a final element at its limit ends the loop's authority over the temperature.

The feedback is negative when the controller action opposes the deviation. A temperature above the set point reduces the heat supply, and a temperature below the set point increases it. Negative feedback returns the temperature toward the set point after a disturbance. Positive feedback would drive the temperature further from the set point and is not used for temperature holding.
